title: MUST YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST BEFORE GOD WILL FORGIVE YOU? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU APPROACH JESUS FOREVER
paragraphs: MUST YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST BEFORE GOD WILL FORGIVE YOU? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU APPROACH JESUS FOREVER

What if the shame you've been carrying has convinced you that God is farther away than He really is? A journey through Scripture, the original Greek and Hebrew, the authority Jesus gave His Church, and the extraordinary grace that opens the way to the Father.
There is a kind of guilt that follows you into the night.
You can laugh with your family. You can attend church. You can sing worship songs, raise your hands, and tell everyone you're doing fine.
But when the noise disappears, something inside you begins whispering.
You know what you did.
And perhaps the most painful question isn't whether you've sinned.
You already know you have.
The question is whether God will still receive you.

Maybe you've wondered whether you need to find a priest before God will listen. Maybe you've been taught that confessing your sins directly to Jesus is enough. Maybe you've heard Christians passionately defending both positions, each opening the same Bible and insisting the other has misunderstood it.
And somewhere between those arguments stands a person who simply wants to be forgiven.
Someone like you.
Someone like me.
Someone who doesn't need another religious shouting match.
Someone who needs to know what Jesus actually said.
So before we answer whether confession to a priest is necessary, we need to travel somewhere uncomfortable.
Not to a modern church building.
Not to a confessional booth.
But to a courtyard in Jerusalem, where a man who loved Jesus had just committed the betrayal he swore he would never commit.
Peter.
The disciple who declared that he would follow Jesus even to death.
The man who walked on water, witnessed miracles, and heard the voice of the Son of God.
And yet, when a servant girl questioned him, his courage collapsed.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 records something devastating:
"And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of Jesus meeting the eyes of the man who had just denied knowing Him.
No sermon.
No public humiliation.
Just a look.
And Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Have you ever had a moment like that?
A moment when you realized that the person you had become was not the person you promised God you would be?

A secret relationship. A hidden addiction. A lie that became another lie. A marriage wounded by betrayal. An angry outburst that shattered someone's trust. A private habit you keep promising to abandon.
And then comes the question.
How do I get back to God?
That question is where our journey begins.
Because the Bible doesn't treat sin as a minor mistake that disappears when we feel better about ourselves.
Sin is serious.
The Hebrew word חָטָא (chata) commonly carries the meaning of sinning or missing the mark. In the Greek New Testament, ἁμαρτία (hamartia) is the ordinary word for sin.
But biblical sin is more than simply failing to achieve our personal potential.
It is rebellion against the holy God who created us. It includes what we do, what we desire, what we neglect, and the ways we refuse His rightful authority.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
The pastor.
The priest.
The church volunteer.
The person reading Scripture every morning.
The person who hasn't entered a church in twenty years.
And yes, the person writing these words.
None of us stands before God on the strength of our own goodness.
Which makes the next question incredibly important.
If every human being is a sinner, who has the authority to bring us back to God?
The answer begins with a word that once shaped Israel's entire worship.
כֹּהֵן — kohen.
Priest.
Under the old covenant, God appointed priests to serve in Israel's sacrificial worship. The high priest had a particularly solemn responsibility connected with the Day of Atonement.
Leviticus 16 describes the sacred rituals through which atonement was made for Israel.
The priest did not invent forgiveness.
He served within the covenantal system God had established.
And the sacrifices pointed beyond themselves.
Hebrews 10:4 declares:
"For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins." (KJV)
Those sacrifices could not accomplish the final, complete removal of sin that humanity desperately needed.
Something greater was coming.
Or rather...
Someone.
When Jesus entered the world, He did not arrive merely to improve religious behavior.
He came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived without sin.
He willingly offered Himself.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And the book of Hebrews identifies Him as our great High Priest.
The Greek word is ἀρχιερεύς — archiereus.
Hebrews 4:14–16 says:
"Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (KJV)
Read that final sentence again.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace."
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because we have earned an audience with heaven.
But because Jesus is our High Priest.
The Greek word translated "boldly" is παρρησία (parrēsia), conveying openness, confidence, or freedom of speech.
It does not mean approaching God arrogantly.
It means approaching Him with confidence grounded in Christ.
And the invitation is extraordinary.
The throne of the holy God is called a throne of grace.
Not because God's holiness has diminished.
But because Jesus has opened the way.

Hebrews 10:19–22 develops this truth further, describing believers as having confidence to enter the holy place through the blood of Jesus and calling them to draw near with sincere hearts and full assurance of faith.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We do not approach God by pretending our sins are small.
We approach Him because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
And this brings us to one of the clearest declarations in the entire New Testament.
First Timothy 2:5:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." (KJV)
In Greek, the central phrase reads:
εἷς γὰρ θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς
Heis gar Theos, heis kai mesitēs Theou kai anthrōpōn, anthrōpos Christos Iēsous.
A faithful rendering is:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus."
The crucial word is μεσίτης — mesitēs.
Mediator.
Someone who stands between parties to bring about reconciliation.
And Paul identifies one ultimate mediator between God and humanity.
Jesus Christ.
Not because pastors have no purpose.
Not because priests are automatically dishonest.
Not because the Church is unnecessary.
But because no human minister can replace the saving work of the crucified and risen Son of God.
Christ alone is the mediator whose sacrificial work reconciles sinners to the Father.
That truth is affirmed across historic Christian traditions, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy, and Protestantism.
But here is where the conversation becomes more complicated.
Because although Christians agree that Jesus is the one saving mediator, they disagree about how He has appointed His Church to minister forgiveness.
And if we want the truth, we must be willing to examine the passages that challenge our assumptions.
After His resurrection, Jesus appeared to His disciples.
John 20:21–23 records:
"Then said Jesus to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost:
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained." (KJV)
Those words cannot simply be ignored.
Jesus truly gave His disciples a commission involving the forgiveness and retention of sins.
The Greek text of John 20:23 includes:
ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας
An tinōn aphēte tas hamartias.
"If you forgive the sins of any..."
The verb ἀφῆτε (aphēte) comes from ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), which can mean to release, remit, or forgive.
The passage speaks of genuine authority entrusted by the risen Christ.
The disagreement concerns how that authority continues to operate in the Church.

Catholic teaching understands this commission as foundational to the sacrament of Penance or Reconciliation, through which bishops and priests exercise a ministry of absolution received through apostolic succession.
Eastern Orthodox Christians also practice sacramental confession to a priest, understanding forgiveness as God's gift and the priest as a minister and witness within the Church's healing ministry.

Many Protestant Christians understand John 20:23 primarily as authority to proclaim the Gospel, declare forgiveness to the repentant, and exercise church discipline according to Christ's Word. Some Protestant traditions also retain private confession and pastoral absolution.
These differences matter.
It would be unfair to claim that Catholics believe priests independently manufacture forgiveness.
Official Catholic teaching identifies God as the source of forgiveness and Christ as the one who reconciles sinners. The priest acts sacramentally in Christ's name, not as a competing savior.
It would also be unfair to claim that Protestants who confess directly to God necessarily reject the importance of the Church, pastoral care, or accountability.

The real theological question is whether Christ instituted individual priestly confession as an ordinarily necessary sacramental means of reconciliation for grave sins committed after baptism, or whether the believer may seek and receive God's forgiveness directly through Christ without such a requirement.
And to answer responsibly, we must examine more Scripture.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
The Greek verb translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen.
It comes from ὁμολογέω (homologeō), meaning to confess, acknowledge, or agree.
In this context, it refers to acknowledging our sins truthfully before God rather than denying or concealing them.
Notice the promise.
"He is faithful and just to forgive us."
God is the one who forgives.
And the verse does not explicitly require the presence of a priest.
That observation is important.
But we should also be careful.

The absence of an explicit priestly requirement in this verse does not, by itself, settle every question about the sacrament of reconciliation. Catholic and Orthodox interpreters read this passage alongside John 20 and the Church's sacramental life.
Nevertheless, 1 John 1:9 unmistakably teaches that forgiveness comes from God and that genuine confession involves truthfulness about our sin.
You cannot heal a wound you insist does not exist.
You cannot honestly repent of a sin you continually defend.
And you cannot build a life of spiritual integrity while maintaining a secret agreement with darkness.
Confession is not an attempt to inform an uninformed God.
He already knows.
It is the surrender of our excuses.
It is when we stop saying, "I had no choice," and begin saying, "Lord, I sinned."
It is when blame finally gives way to repentance.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years confusing feeling guilty with actually turning away from sin.
Those are not the same thing.
Guilt can make you cry.
Repentance changes the direction of your life.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia — means repentance, a change of mind or disposition that, in biblical usage, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
It is not merely regret over consequences.
It is a transformed response to God's truth.
And Scripture shows us what that looks like through another man who committed terrible sin.
King David.
A man described as one after God's own heart.
A man who worshiped, prayed, and wrote psalms.
Yet David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that led to her husband Uriah's death.
His position did not excuse him.
His spiritual history did not protect him from accountability.
And his public reputation could not erase what he had done.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David finally spoke words that broke through his self-deception.
"I have sinned against the LORD." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
Nathan replied:
"The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
Notice the beauty and seriousness of that moment.
David confessed his sin before a prophet who confronted him with God's Word.
But Nathan identified the LORD as the one who had put away David's sin.
And forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
David's story refuses to let us cheapen grace.
God forgives.
But sin can still wound families, destroy trust, and leave consequences that require humility, restitution, and long obedience.
Psalm 51 gives us a window into David's repentance.
"Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight." (Psalm 51:4, KJV)
David was not denying the terrible harm he had done to other people.
He was acknowledging that every sin is ultimately an offense against God.
Later he prayed:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
The verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from ברא (bara), the Hebrew verb "to create."
David was asking God to do something deeper than improve his public image.
He wanted a clean heart.
A work only God could accomplish.
Maybe that is what you need tonight.
Not a better explanation.
Not another promise you already know you cannot keep in your own strength.
Not a religious performance designed to make people think you are holy.
A clean heart.
And now we come to another Scripture that must be taken seriously.
James 5:16 says:
"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." (KJV)
The Greek uses the expression:
ἐξομολογεῖσθε οὖν ἀλλήλοις τὰς ἁμαρτίας
Exomologeisthe oun allēlois tas hamartias.
"Therefore, confess your sins to one another."
The Greek word ἁμαρτίας (hamartias) means "sins." The KJV's "faults" should not be understood as restricting the passage to mere personality weaknesses.
And the reciprocal expression ἀλλήλοις (allēlois) means "to one another."
This passage affirms the importance of confession within the believing community.
We are not called to live as isolated Christians who refuse correction, accountability, prayer, or spiritual support.
Sometimes healing begins when a trembling voice finally says to a trusted believer:
"I need help."
Sometimes repentance requires confessing wrongdoing to the person we have injured.
Sometimes addiction loses its secrecy when a mature Christian walks beside us with prayer, truth, and accountability.
And sometimes pastoral ministry provides the wise spiritual guidance that a struggling believer desperately needs.
But James 5:16 does not explicitly state that every sin must be privately confessed to an ordained priest before God can forgive it.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians see this passage as consistent with the Church's practice of sacramental confession, while many Protestants understand it as a broader command for mutual confession and prayer.
Both the text itself and the differences in interpretation deserve to be acknowledged.
Because the goal should never be to win an argument by pretending difficult verses do not exist.
The goal is to understand God's Word faithfully.
And this brings us to the question many readers have been waiting for.
Can a believer approach God directly through Jesus Christ?
Yes.
Scripture clearly teaches that believers have access to the Father through Christ.
Ephesians 2:18 says:
"For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father." (KJV)
The "him" is Christ.
The Spirit gives access.
The Father receives us.
And Romans 5:1–2 teaches that those justified by faith have peace with God through Jesus Christ and access into grace through Him.
This is not a spiritual loophole.
It is not a rejection of Christian fellowship.
It is the astonishing privilege purchased by the blood of Jesus.
You do not need to persuade Jesus to care about your suffering.
He already gave Himself for sinners.
You do not need to hide your shame until you have become respectable enough to pray.
The Gospel calls you to bring your sin into the light and turn to Christ.
But does this mean priestly confession is unnecessary in every Christian tradition?
Here we must distinguish the direct access all Christians have through Christ from the different teachings about sacramental reconciliation.

The Catholic Church teaches that individual confession and absolution are the ordinary means of reconciliation for Catholics conscious of grave sin after baptism, while also recognizing that perfect contrition, arising from love of God and including the firm intention to receive sacramental confession as soon as possible, can obtain forgiveness of mortal sins before sacramental absolution.
That teaching is found in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, especially paragraphs 1451–1457.
Eastern Orthodox practice also places strong emphasis on confession and absolution within the sacramental life of the Church, though particular pastoral practices differ.

Most evangelical and Reformed Protestants hold that believers may confess directly to God through Jesus Christ and receive forgiveness without priestly absolution. Lutheran and Anglican traditions include varying forms of private confession and absolution while affirming that Christ is the source of forgiveness.

Therefore, the statement "all Christians must confess every sin to a priest or God will never forgive them" does not accurately represent the whole of historic Christianity, and it oversimplifies even Catholic teaching.

Likewise, the statement "confessing sins to a priest is always unbiblical" goes beyond what can be established without engaging seriously with John 20:23, James 5, and the history of Christian interpretation.
The clearest shared biblical truth is this:
No priest, pastor, church leader, or religious institution can replace Jesus Christ as the Savior and mediator of sinners.
And every genuine ministry of reconciliation must ultimately depend on Him.
There is another scene in Scripture that reveals something extraordinary about God's mercy.
Jesus told a story about a son who demanded his inheritance, left his father's house, and wasted everything in reckless living.
Eventually, the money disappeared.
The friends disappeared.
The comfort disappeared.
And the young man found himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Luke 15 says that he came to himself.
He decided to return home.
But he did not come back with an impressive résumé.
He came back with a confession.
"Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son." (Luke 15:21, KJV)
Imagine him walking that road.
Every step reminding him of what he had thrown away.
Every memory accusing him.
Every approaching landmark bringing him closer to the father he had dishonored.
Perhaps he rehearsed his confession again and again.
Perhaps he wondered whether the door would be shut.
Perhaps he feared that his father's face would be filled with disgust.
But Jesus said something that still shakes the human heart.
"When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." (Luke 15:20, KJV)
He was still a great way off.
And the father ran.
Not because the son's rebellion was acceptable.
Not because repentance was meaningless.
But because the father's mercy was greater than the son's expectation.
The son returned confessing his sin.
The father received him with compassion.
This parable is not a technical manual for resolving every sacramental disagreement.
It is a revelation of the Father's heart toward the repentant.
And some of us have spent years imagining God as less merciful than the Father Jesus described.
We picture Him standing at the door with folded arms, waiting to see whether our tears are convincing enough.
But the cross tells a different story.
God's mercy is not reluctant.
It is costly.
Jesus did not die because our sins were insignificant.
He died because they were so serious that reconciliation required His saving sacrifice.
And grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
Grace is the power that calls us home.
Now remember Peter.
The man who denied Jesus.
The man who wept bitterly.
The man whose confidence had shattered.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter beside the Sea of Galilee.
John 21 records Jesus asking him three times whether he loved Him.
Three questions.
Three opportunities for Peter to affirm his love.
And Jesus entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
What an extraordinary restoration.
Peter's failure was real.
His tears were real.
His need for grace was real.
But his denial did not become the final sentence of his story.
Jesus restored him and called him to serve.
And that is the message some wounded believer needs to hear today.
Your sin is not small.
Your choices matter.
The people you have hurt matter.
Repentance matters.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your worst failure does not have to become your final identity.
The same Peter who denied Jesus would later proclaim Christ publicly.
Not because Peter discovered that he was strong enough.
But because the risen Christ had not abandoned him.
That is what redemption looks like.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
But watching grace write a future that sin could never have produced.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the scandal in your life is something nobody knows.
Perhaps it is the marriage you damaged.
The child you neglected.
The person you betrayed.
The secret you buried.
The faith you almost abandoned.
Or perhaps the scandal is quieter.
You have attended church for years, but somewhere along the way, you stopped believing that God actually wanted you near Him.
You learned the vocabulary of religion.
But lost the wonder of grace.
You know how to bow your head.
But you have forgotten how to open your heart.
And the invitation of Hebrews is still standing.
Come boldly to the throne of grace.
Not carelessly.
Not defiantly.
Not with a plan to continue cherishing the sin that crucified your Savior.
Come repentantly.
Come honestly.
Come trusting the finished work of Jesus Christ.

If you are Catholic or Orthodox, this direct approach to Christ need not be understood as a rejection of the sacramental confession taught by your Church. Seek the Lord sincerely and follow the pastoral discipline of your tradition with an informed conscience.
If you are Protestant, do not confuse the privilege of direct confession with permission to reject correction, accountability, or the ministry of fellow believers.
And wherever you worship, never let a human minister become a substitute for personal faith in Jesus.
A church leader may counsel you.
A priest may minister reconciliation according to his Church's understanding.
A pastor may proclaim God's promises.
A trusted believer may pray beside you.
But Jesus is the one who died and rose again.
Jesus is the one who saves.
Jesus is the one through whom we come to the Father.
And there is no salvation apart from Him.
Acts 4:12 declares:
"Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." (KJV)
That name is Jesus.
Not your denomination.
Not your religious achievements.
Not your record of charitable works.
Not your ability to produce perfect words of confession.
Jesus.
And if you are wondering what to do right now, begin with the truth.
Tell God what you have done.
Do not soften it.
Do not disguise it.
Do not blame someone else.
Ask for His mercy through Jesus Christ.
Trust His promise of forgiveness.
Turn away from your sin.
Where possible and appropriate, seek reconciliation with people you have harmed. Make restitution where you can. Receive correction. Seek spiritual counsel. Pursue accountability.
And when you fall, do not make hiding your new home.
First John 2:1 says:
"My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." (KJV)
The Greek word for "advocate" is παράκλητος — paraklētos.
It describes someone called alongside to help or plead another's cause.
Here, Jesus Christ the righteous is identified as our advocate with the Father.
Notice John's balance.
"That ye sin not."
And then:
"If any man sin, we have an advocate."
Holiness matters.
And mercy remains available to those who turn to Christ.
John is not encouraging us to sin.
He is telling believers where to look when they do.
Look to Jesus.
And maybe that is where the deepest transformation begins.
Not when we become obsessed with proving that our particular tradition has won an argument.
But when we become overwhelmed again by the glory of the Savior whom all faithful Christian ministry must proclaim.
Because the purpose of forgiveness is not merely to relieve emotional discomfort.
It is reconciliation with God.
A restored relationship.
A transformed life.
A heart increasingly surrendered to the Lord.
And this truth is too important to keep trapped inside one person's screen.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who still believes their past makes them unreachable.
Someone who thinks God is finished with them.
Someone who has been wounded by religion and now struggles to distinguish the failures of people from the character of Jesus.
It can be the beginning of restoration.
And if this message has touched something you have been carrying in silence, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not need to disclose private sins publicly. You can also share a testimony, a Scripture that helped you, or a sincere question about confession and forgiveness.
Let the comments become a place where believers encourage one another toward repentance, truth, and grace rather than attacking one another over denominational differences.
There may come a night when guilt returns, when old memories become loud, or when someone you love asks how forgiveness through Jesus actually works.
You may need these Scriptures again.
It is about following a perfect Savior.
Not because God measures your love for Him by a monthly payment.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price of our redemption. No financial contribution can purchase what His blood has freely secured.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of Christian generosity and stewardship.
Every month, creating biblical teaching, sharing Scripture, developing discipleship materials, and reaching more people requires time, resources, and continued commitment.

It can be a voluntary expression of your giving to Christian ministry, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, family, and those in need. Whether you regard it as part of your charitable offerings is a matter of prayerful stewardship; it should never be presented as a compulsory biblical tithe or a substitute for your church's responsibilities.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not grudgingly.
Not under pressure.
Not out of fear that God will withhold His love.
But freely.
From a willing heart.
These products are simply resources and reminders. They do not make anyone more spiritual, and purchasing them is never a measure of devotion to Christ.
Pray for the ministry.
Sometimes the message you share becomes the Scripture someone reads at the exact moment they were about to surrender to despair.
We cannot promise what God will do through every post.
But we can faithfully proclaim the Gospel and trust Him with the fruit.
Because in the end, the mission is not to build a community that worships a ministry.
It is to help build a community that worships Jesus.
And that brings us back to the person standing in the shadows, wondering whether God will listen.
Perhaps that person is still you.
You have read the Scriptures.
You have seen the different Christian interpretations.
You have heard the invitation to repentance.
But one question remains.
After everything I have done, will Jesus still receive me?
Listen to His own words in John 6:37:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
Those words do not make repentance unnecessary.
They reveal the gracious heart of the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
You may have spent years running.
You may have wasted opportunities.
You may have broken promises that once seemed sacred.
You may have confessed the same struggle so many times that you are ashamed to speak about it again.
But the answer is not to become comfortable with sin.
And it is not to abandon hope.
The answer is to come to Christ.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the brokenness.
Bring Him the life you cannot repair by yourself.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust Him as Savior.
Follow Him as Lord.
And let His grace teach you to walk in the light.
Because the greatest miracle is not that sinners can find the right religious words.
It is that the holy Son of God gave His life to reconcile sinners to the Father.
The cross was not a decoration.
The resurrection was not a metaphor.
And grace is not a sentimental excuse for remaining unchanged.
Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again.
That is the Gospel.
That is our hope.
That is why repentance is possible.
That is why forgiveness is more than wishful thinking.
And that is why the final word over a repentant sinner's life does not have to be the scandal of yesterday.
It can be the grace of Jesus Christ.
The sin you are afraid to bring into the light is not hidden from Jesus—and the Savior who already knows the truth is still calling you to come to Him.
